```{python}
import polars as pl 
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
import polars.selectors as cs
# add the additional libraries you need to import for ML here

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

data_url = "https://byuidatascience.github.io/DS250-Course-Polars/Data/StarWars_with_emails.csv"
```

<!-- The first 10 rows are not part of the datset we need.

The columns headers are split across two rows. We need to clean and simplify the column headers-->

```{python}
# Read in and tidy up the first row
a = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 10, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))
# Note the non-aschii character in the column "Do you consider yourself to be a fan of the Expanded Universe". (column AF if you open it in Excel). 

# BTW: Detecting what it is and where can be difficult

# Lossy means that invalid utf8 values are replaced with � characters. When using other encodings than utf8 or utf8-lossy, the input is first decoded in memory with python. Defaults to utf8...ignore_errors = True does not replace the non-utf8 character with a blank space like you would hope

a[2] = "seen_any" #simply overwrite the value at index 2

# Rather than changing each column header manually,
# here we use regex to apply changes more efficiently
a = (
  a.str.replace(r".+seen.+", "seen_")
   .str.replace(r".+rank.+", "rank_")
   .str.replace(r"(.+favorably.+)", "fav_")
   .fill_null(strategy = "forward")

   .str.replace("\uFFFD+", "") #this gets rid of the question marks in a diamond characters 
   .str.strip_chars()
   .str.to_lowercase()
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .str.replace(r"location(.+)", "location")

)
a[3] = "star_wars_fan"
a[30] = "who_shot_first"
a[31] = "know_expanded_universe"
a[32] = "expanded_universe_fan"
a[33] = "star_trek_fan"
```

<!-- Combine series q and a into one series to be used as column names-->

```{python}
b = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 11, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))

b = (
  b.str.replace(r"Star Wars: (Episode \w+) .+", "${1}")
   .str.replace("Response", "")
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .fill_null("")
   .str.strip_chars()
)

```

```{python}
#Now combine the two series, each of which contains part of the desired column header
new_names = (a + b).to_list()

# Read in the data, skipping over the column header rows
# and use 'new_names' as the column headers
df = pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=12, has_header=False, new_columns = new_names )
```

## Executive Summary

_This is to show if people consider themselves to be Star Wars fans. Have they seen the movies? Do they know the characters? Are they also fans of Star Trek?_



## Methods

_The survey data required several preprocessing steps before it could be used for machine learning. The first two rows of the dataset were combined to create meaningful column names, and unnecessary text was removed from the headers. Missing values in categorical variables were replaced with an "Unknown" category so that responses would not be discarded._

_The response variable for this analysis was whether the respondent considered themselves to be a Star Wars fan. This variable was converted into a binary target variable, where "Yes" was coded as 1 and "No" was coded as 0._

_Because nearly all survey responses were categorical, one-hot encoding was used to convert them into numeric variables that could be used by the machine learning algorithm. Identifier columns and the target variable were removed from the predictor dataset before training._

_The cleaned data was divided into training and testing sets using a 75%/25% split. A Random Forest classifier was selected because it performs well with many categorical predictors and can model complex relationships without requiring extensive feature engineering. Model performance was evaluated using a classification report, and permutation importance was used to determine which variables contributed most to the model's predictions._

```{python}
## Methods
# Stretch Requirement
# Validate the dataset by recreating two visuals from the original article

# -------------------------
# Visual 1: Have you seen each Star Wars movie?
# -------------------------

seen_cols = [
    "seen_Episode_I",
    "seen_Episode_II",
    "seen_Episode_III",
    "seen_Episode_IV",
    "seen_Episode_V",
    "seen_Episode_VI"
]

seen_plot = (
    df.select(seen_cols)
      .unpivot(variable_name="Movie", value_name="Seen")
      .filter(pl.col("Seen") == "Yes")
      .group_by("Movie")
      .len()
      .with_columns(
          (
              pl.col("len") /
              df.height * 100
          ).alias("Percent")
      )
)

ggplot(
    seen_plot,
    aes(
        x="Movie",
        y="Percent"
    )
) + \
geom_bar(
    stat="identity",
    fill="#4E79A7"
) + \
labs(
    title="Have Seen Each Star Wars Film",
    subtitle="Percent of respondents",
    x="Movie",
    y="Percent"
) + \
theme(axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1))


# -------------------------
# Visual 2: Are you a Star Trek fan?
# -------------------------

trek_plot = (
    df.group_by("star_trek_fan")
      .len()
      .with_columns(
          (
              pl.col("len") /
              pl.col("len").sum() * 100
          ).alias("Percent")
      )
      .sort("Percent", descending=True)
)

ggplot(
    trek_plot,
    aes(
        x="star_trek_fan",
        y="Percent"
    )
) + \
geom_bar(
    stat="identity",
    fill="#E15759"
) + \
labs(
    title="Do You Consider Yourself a Star Trek Fan?",
    subtitle="Survey responses",
    x="Response",
    y="Percent"
)

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

# Create target variable
df = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("star_wars_fan")
      .fill_null("No")
      .replace({
          "Yes": 1,
          "No": 0
      })
      .alias("target")
)

# Remove columns that should not be predictors
drop_cols = [
    "respondentid",
    "star_wars_fan",
    "target"
]

X = df.drop(drop_cols)
y = df["target"].to_numpy()

# Replace missing values
X = X.with_columns(
    cs.string().fill_null("Unknown")
)

# Convert categorical variables into dummy variables
X = X.to_dummies()

# Convert to NumPy
X_np = X.to_numpy()

# Split the data
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_np,
    y,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=42
)

# Train the Random Forest model
rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=200,
    random_state=42
)

rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
```


## Results

_The Random Forest model was evaluated using a 75/25 train-test split. The classification report summarizes the model's precision, recall, F1-score, and overall accuracy. Permutation importance was then used to identify which survey responses were the strongest predictors of whether a respondent considered themselves to be a Star Wars fan._

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
## Results
# Make predictions
predictions = rf.predict(X_test)

# Display classification report
print(classification_report(y_test, predictions))

# Calculate permutation importance
importance = permutation_importance(
    rf,
    X_test,
    y_test,
    n_repeats=3,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Create a Polars DataFrame of feature importance
importance_df = (
    pl.DataFrame({
        "Feature": X.columns,
        "Importance": importance.importances_mean
    })
    .sort("Importance", descending=True)
)

# Display the 15 most important features
importance_df.head(15)

# Plot feature importance
ggplot(
    importance_df.head(15),
    aes(
        x="Importance",
        y="Feature"
    )
) + \
geom_bar(stat="identity") + \
labs(
    title="Top 15 Most Important Features",
    x="Permutation Importance",
    y="Feature"
)
```

The model identified several survey questions that were especially useful for predicting whether someone is a Star Wars fan. Variables related to whether respondents had seen the films, their opinions of the movies, and their favorite characters tended to have the highest importance values. These findings suggest that movie experience and opinions are much stronger predictors than demographic information alone.


## Results

_The most common result in the permutation importance analysis was that respondents who had seen the Star Wars films were more likely to identify as fans._
